title: This Ancient Fish's Brain Holds Clues to How Animals First Walked on Land
summary: How did fish ever learn to walk on land? A fossil from Antarctica is giving us new clues. Meet Koharalepis jarviki, a big predatory fish that lived 380 million years ago during the Devonian Period—the 'Age of Fishes.' It grew about as long as a baseball bat and hunted smaller creatures in ancient rivers. Scientists at Flinders University in Australia used super-powerful neutron imaging to look inside its fossilized skull without breaking it. What they found was amazing. The fish's brain was similar to those of the very first animals that crawled out of the water onto land. It even had special openings on top of its skull, like a built-in skylight, to gulp air from the surface. Inside its brain, there was an organ that could sense light and help it keep a daily rhythm, kind of like a body clock. Because its eyes were small, it probably relied on other senses to ambush prey. This fish belongs to a family called Canowindridae, which links ancient Australia and Antarctica when they were part of the same supercontinent. The fossil is the only one of its kind with the inside skull bones preserved, so it's a rare treasure. By studying it, scientists can better understand the step-by-step changes that let some fish eventually evolve into four-legged land animals—and eventually, into us.
why_it_matters: This discovery helps explain how our own distant ancestors moved from water to land, a key moment in the story of life on Earth.

background_read: During the Devonian Period, fish ruled the waters and some were just starting to develop limbs to crawl onto land.
The fossil was found in Antarctica, but 380 million years ago Antarctica was warm and connected to Australia in a supercontinent called Gondwana.
Scientists at Flinders University (a university in Australia) used special imaging to study the skull without damaging the rare fossil.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists from Flinders University and the ancient fish Koharalepis jarviki
WHAT: The fish's brain had air-gulping holes and light-sensing organs, linking it to early land animals
WHERE: The fossil was discovered in Antarctica, a former part of Gondwana
WHY: To trace the evolutionary steps that let fish eventually walk on land

perspectives.description: This fossil fills a gap in the tree of life, showing that fish developed land-animal-like brains earlier than thought.
Since it's the only fossil of its kind with preserved skull bones, scientists are careful not to jump to conclusions about all fish.
New imaging techniques like neutron scanning may let researchers study other delicate fossils without damage, leading to more discoveries.
